then.text: We rehearse in the Institute now. It is cold, and the acoustic is a wardrobe. We have sung worse, and in worse, and not often.
We sang on a scaffold in March. The altos said it was the best acoustic yet, which I did not take as a compliment.
We stop at nine, and Kieran's tenants send down tea on Thursdays. It is not what I would have chosen, and it is better than I deserve.
Eirlys has had you in the vestry, has she? Then I know what you will ask. Sit down. Not on the third pew.
A male voice choir is not a thing you can move into a hall. It is the roof. The sound goes up, comes back and arrives at the back row as a chord. Forty men in a cold hall sing at the floor.

I am not a deacon and I do not decide the sale. I would only say: the choir is the best argument for the chapel, and Kieran is the best argument for the valley, and I like him, and I will not forgive either of you.
We would manage. The hymns survive anything. I would just like it to be said that I minded.

else.text: About the chapel? Hear Kieran at the Institute first. Then come and ask me what a choir loses. I will have a better answer if you have heard what a lad needs.
A concert at the pithead, you say? Against a theme park? Bless you, that's the most sensible idea I've heard since they let the altos choose a hymn.
Bethania can fill a chapel. To fill a square we need the Swansea choir as well, and that means Gwenllian Pugh. She does not give her forty voices to just anybody.

then.text: She's already written to me about you. 'The one with the Welsh cakes,' she says. That's a reference, that is. Gwenllian's choir will be there on the night, and mine.
Two choirs are promised for the pithead.

else.text: Have you met her? Swansea, usually, or Cardiff if she's after a statue to conduct. Get to know her. Welsh cakes, still warm. Then she'll sing.

then.text: Practice is Thursday and Saturday. If you ever hear a roof coming off in the Rhondda, that's us.
Four parts at last: first tenor, second tenor, baritone and a proper bass. Four parts and one conductor with a very sore throat.
The eisteddfod pavilion is packed to the rafters. Elwyn raises his baton. For a moment there is no sound at all.
Then forty men breathe in together, and the roof lifts. The Cwm Rhondda goes up through the canvas like a rocket.
Second place! Second! We beat the Treorchy boys by a whisker and a bad key change. Here. Take the medal. It's yours as much as ours.

else.text: We're still a voice short. Have you tried the baker, the Merthyr pub, the Workmen's Hall and Big Pit?
We're still a voice short. Have you tried the baker, the Merthyr pub, the Workmen's Hall and Big Pit?
We're still a voice short. Have you tried the baker, the Merthyr pub, the Workmen's Hall and Big Pit?
We're still a voice short. Have you tried the baker, the Merthyr pub, the Workmen's Hall and Big Pit?
Bore da. Elwyn Prosser, conductor of the Bethania Male Voice Choir. We've got the National Eisteddfod in a fortnight and we're a quartet short.

I need four voices: a first tenor, a second tenor, a baritone and a bass. I've heard rumours of singers in the bakehouse over the road, in a pub in Merthyr, in the Workmen's Hall at Blaenavon, and underground in Big Pit.
Find them for me. And tell them they won't be paid, but there'll be tea.

rhn_organist.text: Nineteen hymns, six anthems and a Welsh Wedding March. I could play any of them in my sleep, and I have, in the sermon.
A male voice choir needs four parts: first tenor, second tenor, baritone, bass. Miss any one and you can hear the hole in it, like a missing tooth.

then.text: I walked past on Sunday and there were curtains in the windows. Real curtains. It is a strange thing, seeing your chapel have a front door with a number on it.
Nine of us and a rota and a hundred and forty pounds a month in the tin. We are not dead. We are not well, either. But we sang on Sunday and the roof held.
The flats are full and the chapel is still a chapel. I have noticed that nobody is entirely happy, which I have decided to take as a good sign.
Sell it, then. To a lad who sat in the third pew on a Sunday afternoon and complained about the sermon. I will tell the members what you said.
Keep it. Nine of us and a roof. I will tell the members what you said, and then I will go and look for a ladder.
Sell the back and keep the front. Well. I would have liked to have thought of it. I will tell the members.
The post for the terrace comes to Bryn Terrace, where the kettle always is. Word will come, one way or another.

Well? You have heard Kieran and you have heard Elwyn. We are four to four, and I am the ninth, and I cannot say, because I have been secretary for thirty-one years and they would say I only wanted what I wanted.
What do you tell Eirlys?
options: Sell it to Kieran, for flats
Keep it, and raise the money
Sell the schoolroom, keep the chapel

then.text: Flats. Six of them, and the front kept as it is. And the choir in a cold hall, and the organ in a van.
I will tell the members. Come to the terrace for the post when it is done.
Keep it. Nine of us, a tin and a roof with a hole in it. And not one person under fifty to hold the ladder.
I will tell the members. Come to the terrace for the post when it is done.
The old Sunday school at the back to Kieran, for two flats, and the chapel for the choir. The teas move into the vestry, and the choir stops at nine, or the flats will complain.
I will tell the members. Come to the terrace for the post when it is done.
Take your time. The roof will not, but you can.

else.text: Elwyn Prosser is at the front, when he is not in the pulpit pretending it is a podium. Ask him what the choir would lose.
Kieran Rees. He is over at the Institute, in the reading room, with his plans. Hear him out. He is not what you think.
Eirlys Bevan, secretary. Mind the third pew, it complains.

There are nine of us on a Sunday now. In my mother's day there were four hundred, and a gallery, and a sermon that went on until the beef burned. The roof needs more than we have, and so does the boiler, and so do I.

A builder has made us an offer. It is a good one, for flats. The members meet on Sunday and we are four against four, and I am the ninth. Would you hear everyone out and tell me what you think? You are nobody's cousin.

w55w_ladder.text: Roof. I am the one who holds the ladder. I am sixty-eight, so that tells you where the next generation is.
The thermometer in the porch says forty per cent. I say that is rounding.

w55w_father.text: We have the flat at the back, the old Sunday school. The baby sleeps through the sermon, which I am told is a first for that room.
The choir stops at nine. I thank them every Thursday. I do not say it out loud.
